title: The Stock Market Is Being Used as a Dumping Ground
note: EP021 — explainer (By the Numbers, row 11). IPOs/SPACs as insider exits onto retail. Free Imgflip memes; 5 new motifs (ipopop, bagholder, exitramp, lockupcliff, hotpotato); meaningful-phrase citations. Target 12–15 min.

scenes.narration: Here's the pitch you've heard a thousand times. A hot company goes public. You buy in early, on day one, and ride it to the moon. Get in before everyone else.
It feels like you're being let in on the ground floor. But step back and ask one question almost nobody asks: who, exactly, is selling you those shares?
Because an IPO isn't really the start of the story. For the people who got in truly early, it's the exit. The day they finally get to cash out — by selling to you.
scenes.caption: an IPO is an exit — for insiders

scenes.narration: You think you're getting in at the beginning. Often, you're buying at the moment the smart money has decided it's time to leave.
And the data is brutal. On average, newly public companies have tended to underperform the broader market in the years right after they list.
Look no further than the last big boom. The vast majority of the companies that went public at the 2021 peak later traded well below their starting price.
scenes.sub: of 2021's listings later fell below their IPO price

scenes.narration: The 'ground floor' is a story. By the time it's offered to you, the elevator has usually already gone up — with the insiders on it.
So let's look at how the stock market quietly became a place not just to invest — but to dump overpriced shares onto the public.
scenes.heading: The Stock Market as a Dumping Ground
scenes.sub: You're on the other side of the smartest sellers in the room.

scenes.narration: Start with what an IPO actually is. A company's shares get sold to the public for the very first time.
The official reason is noble: the company raises money to grow — new factories, new hires, paying down debt. And sometimes, that's genuinely what happens.
A bank underwrites it — guaranteeing the sale, setting the price, and lining up the big buyers in advance.
But here's the quiet split most people miss. There are two very different kinds of shares being sold that day.
Primary shares are new — and that money goes to the company. Secondary shares are old — existing stakes that insiders are selling, where the money goes straight into their pockets.
And who are those insiders? The venture capitalists, the funds, the founders, and the early employees who backed it years ago.
For them, the IPO is payday. After years locked into a private company, this is the door that finally lets them turn paper wealth into real cash.
scenes.caption: the insiders' payday

scenes.narration: In plenty of IPOs, most of the shares on offer aren't even new. They're existing shares, being sold by insiders who are quietly heading for the door.
Founders and funds who paid pennies a share years ago get to sell to you at the very top, pocketing the entire gap. That gap is the whole reason for the timing.
scenes.caption: bought for pennies, sold at the top

scenes.narration: So on the single day you're most excited to buy, the people who know the company best are often the ones most eager to sell. Hold that thought.
Now layer on the second trick: timing. Because when a company goes public matters enormously — and it's chosen to benefit the seller, not you.
scenes.heading: The Timing

scenes.narration: Markets move in long waves of optimism and fear. IPOs cluster, overwhelmingly, into the optimistic ones.
It makes total sense — for the seller. If you're offloading something, you do it when buyers are euphoric and prices are high. That's just good business.
But a high price for the seller is, by definition, an expensive price for the buyer. You're being invited in at precisely the most expensive moment.
scenes.caption: high for them = expensive for you

scenes.narration: And remember whose job it is to set the price. The bank — which earns a fat fee on the total amount raised. So it is quietly cheering for the highest price the market will swallow.
Everyone advising on the deal gets paid more when it prices higher. Almost nobody in that room is paid to protect you, the buyer.
scenes.caption: priced for the seller

scenes.narration: Then there's the famous first-day 'pop' — when a stock jumps the moment it starts trading. It looks like proof you should've gotten in.
scenes.caption: the first-day pop

scenes.narration: But watch who actually catches that pop. The banks hand the opening shares to their favored clients, who flip them for an instant profit — before you can even click buy.
By the time an ordinary investor can buy, the easy pop is already gone. You're buying at the high, from someone who just bought at the low, minutes ago.
A lot of this runs on a simple, old idea: that you can buy something overpriced, as long as a 'greater fool' will buy it from you for more.
An overhyped new stock gets passed from hand to hand, each buyer betting someone dumber is right behind them — until, suddenly, nobody is.
scenes.caption: until there's no greater fool left

scenes.narration: It's the oldest trade on Wall Street: excited newcomers rushing in at the top, while the people in the know quietly slip out the back.
scenes.memeBottom: retail chasing hype as insiders exit

scenes.narration: There's even a blunt nickname for the buyers who show up at the top. 'Exit liquidity.' You are the pool of fresh money the early investors get to cash out into.
Which brings us to the single most revealing clue in the whole IPO machine: the lock-up.
scenes.heading: The Lock-Up

scenes.narration: For a set window after the IPO — usually about ninety to a hundred and eighty days — the big insiders are legally barred from selling their shares.
Think about why that rule even has to exist. It's there because, left unchecked, insiders would dump everything on day one — and everyone knows it.
So the lock-up props up the price for a few months, keeping the stock scarce while the hype is loudest. Then the clock runs out.
And on the day the lock-up expires, a flood of insider shares can finally hit the market all at once — and the price very often falls off a cliff.
scenes.caption: lock-up expires → the dump

scenes.narration: It's one of the most reliable patterns on Wall Street. If you want to know what insiders really think of the stock, don't read the press release — watch what they do the moment they're allowed to sell.
And the person holding the shares when the music stops? Usually the last one to the party. The retail investor, left holding the bag.
scenes.caption: retail: left holding the bag

scenes.narration: That lock-up window is usually ninety to a hundred and eighty days. Mark it on a calendar, and you can often watch the dump coming from a mile away.
scenes.sub: before insiders are free to sell

scenes.narration: Over and over, hyped stocks drift along, then drop sharply right around the week their insiders are finally allowed to sell. That's not a coincidence. That's the schedule.
The press release says 'long-term vision.' The lock-up calendar says 'selling in ninety days.' When they disagree, believe the calendar.
scenes.caption: believe the calendar, not the hype

scenes.narration: Underneath all of this sits one unfair advantage that colors everything: information.
scenes.heading: The Information Gap

scenes.narration: Economists have a clean term for it. An information asymmetry — where one side of a deal knows far more than the other.
The insiders have lived inside the company for years. They know the real customers, the real margins, the real problems. You get a glossy document.
That document is the prospectus — the official disclosure every IPO must publish for potential buyers.
And buried deep inside it, in the 'risk factors,' is often a startlingly honest list of everything that could go wrong — written by lawyers, read by almost no one.
Which leaves the one question that cuts through all the hype. If this company is such a sure thing, why are the people who know it best so eager to sell it to you?
scenes.memeBottom: if it's so great, why are they selling?

scenes.narration: Sit with that question, because it is the whole episode. Nobody willingly sells the golden goose. They sell the bird they quietly suspect has already laid its best eggs.
The insider's real choice is simple: keep owning a great company — or sell it to the public at the richest price it may ever see.
scenes.memeBottom: or sell it high to the public

scenes.narration: If you want to see the dumping ground at its purest, look at what happened in 2020 and 2021. Enter the SPAC.
scenes.heading: The SPAC Era

scenes.narration: A SPAC is a 'blank check' company — a shell with no business at all, that raises money from the public first, and goes looking for a company to buy later.
Read that again. You hand over your money, and only afterward do they go find something to spend it on. You're trusting a blank check.
They were sold with star power — famous athletes, celebrities, and star investors lending their names to make a shell company feel like a sure bet.
scenes.caption: sold with celebrity hype

scenes.narration: And the people who set up the SPAC — the sponsors — handed themselves a staggering deal for doing it.
The sponsor typically pockets around twenty percent of the company — the 'promote' — for a tiny upfront sum. A fortune, almost regardless of how the deal performs.
So the incentive was simple and brutal: do a deal, any deal, and get paid. Whether it was a good deal for the public was almost beside the point.
scenes.caption: do any deal, get paid

scenes.narration: In 2021, this hit a frenzy — hundreds of SPACs raised record sums, often merging with companies that had little revenue and big promises.
Then reality arrived. As a group, post-merger SPAC stocks went on to lose most of their value — a textbook transfer of money from the public to the sponsors.
scenes.caption: then they crashed

scenes.narration: It was the dumping ground stripped of all disguise: hype on the way in, collapse on the way out, and insiders paid either way.
scenes.memeBottom: the public: we held the bag

scenes.narration: And when the SPAC bubble burst, the lawsuits came. Several celebrities who had promoted these deals were sued or fined for failing to disclose they were paid to hype them.
And the numbers were grim. Studies of companies that went public through SPACs found many lost well over half their value within a year of the merger.
scenes.sub: the value a typical de-SPAC later lost

scenes.narration: Every one of these manias ends the same way. The asset gets passed along, hand to hand, until it finally lands with whoever believed the story the longest.
scenes.caption: the last believer always loses

scenes.narration: Now, in fairness, let's not throw out the whole stock market. It isn't all a scam.
scenes.heading: To Be Fair

scenes.narration: At its best, the stock market does something genuinely vital: it lets businesses raise money, and lets ordinary people own a slice of them.
Plenty of IPOs are real, growing companies that used the money to build something lasting. Buying great businesses and holding them has made patient investors wealthy.
And after the IPO, most trading happens in the secondary market — investors buying and selling with each other, discovering a fair price over time.
The problem isn't the market itself. It's the one specific moment — the IPO — when the deck is tilted hardest toward the person doing the selling.
And here's the quiet irony. The boring path usually wins. Owning the whole market through a low-cost index fund beats chasing shiny new listings for almost everyone.
You don't have to pick the one new needle. You can own the entire haystack, cheaply — and simply skip the part of the market that's tilted hardest against you.
scenes.caption: own the haystack, skip the hype

scenes.narration: So what do you actually do with all this? It comes down to a few simple, slightly cynical habits.
scenes.heading: How to Not Be the Fool

scenes.narration: First, always ask who is selling, and why they're selling right now. If the best-informed people are rushing for the exit, that tells you something.
Second, treat the first-day hype as a warning sign, not a buy signal. The louder the launch, the more someone wants you excited.
scenes.memeBottom: is a sell signal, not a buy

scenes.narration: Third, watch the lock-up calendar. A wave of insider selling is often scheduled, in plain sight, a few months after the hype peaks.
And fourth — you almost never have to buy on day one. A good company will still be a good company in six months, after the fireworks fade and the real price shows up.
Because the market is really two machines wearing one suit. A place to invest in businesses — and a place to quietly offload risk onto the public.
scenes.caption: invest… or be sold to

scenes.narration: And we have absolutely seen this movie before. In the dot-com bubble, companies with no profits listed into a frenzy, insiders sold, and the public was left holding the wreckage.
The costumes change — dot-coms, SPACs, whatever's hot next. The trade underneath never does: informed sellers, excited buyers, and a price set right at the top.
scenes.caption: same pattern, new decade

scenes.narration: So remember the pattern. Insiders sell high. Banks flip the pop. Lock-ups hide the dump. And the hype is loudest exactly when the risk is greatest.
On the other side of your exciting IPO buy sits the most informed, best-resourced seller you will ever face. That's the whole game in one sentence.
So the next time a glossy new stock promises you the ground floor, you'll ask the only question that matters: if this is the ground floor, why is everyone so keen to get off?
None of this means never invest. It means always know which seat you're in. In an IPO, you are almost always the buyer — sitting directly across the table from the house.
